## Introduction

Six participants performed barbell lifts while wearing accelerometers on the belt, forearm, arm and dumbbell. Each lift was done one correct way (class **A**) and four common incorrect ways (classes **B–E**). The goal is to predict the `classe` variable from the sensor readings. This report compares three models, estimates the out-of-sample error on a held-out validation set, and predicts 20 unlabeled test cases.

## Libraries

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(caret)
library(rattle)
library(corrplot)
set.seed(4234)
```

## Loading and cleaning the data

The data files are downloaded on first run.

```{r load}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
base_url <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/"
for (f in c("pml-training.csv", "pml-testing.csv")) {
  path <- file.path("data", f)
  if (!file.exists(path)) download.file(paste0(base_url, f), path)
}

training_set <- read.csv("data/pml-training.csv")
test_set     <- read.csv("data/pml-testing.csv")
dim(training_set)
dim(test_set)
```

Three cleaning steps reduce 160 columns to 53:

1. Drop columns that are more than 90% missing. These are summary statistics recorded only once per time window.
2. Drop the first seven columns: row ID, participant name, timestamps and window indicators. They identify a recording rather than describe the movement, and would leak information.
3. Drop near-zero-variance predictors.

```{r clean}
training_set <- training_set[, colMeans(is.na(training_set)) < 0.9]
training_set <- training_set[, -c(1:7)]

zero_var <- nearZeroVar(training_set)
training_set <- training_set[, -zero_var]
dim(training_set)
```

A 70/30 stratified split creates a validation set for estimating out-of-sample error.

```{r split}
in_train <- createDataPartition(y = training_set$classe, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train <- training_set[in_train, ]
valid <- training_set[-in_train, ]
```

## Model 1: Decision tree

All models use 3-fold cross-validation for tuning.

```{r tree}
control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 3, verboseIter = FALSE)

decision_tree <- train(classe ~ ., data = train, method = "rpart",
                       trControl = control, tuneLength = 5)
fancyRpartPlot(decision_tree$finalModel)

cm_tree <- confusionMatrix(predict(decision_tree, valid), factor(valid$classe))
cm_tree
```

A single tree reaches only about 55% accuracy. It struggles to separate the four incorrect techniques (B–D).

## Model 2: Random forest

```{r rf}
rf_model <- train(classe ~ ., data = train, method = "rf",
                  trControl = control, tuneLength = 5)

cm_rf <- confusionMatrix(predict(rf_model, valid), factor(valid$classe))
cm_rf
```

## Model 3: Gradient boosting

```{r gbm}
gbm_model <- train(classe ~ ., data = train, method = "gbm",
                   trControl = control, tuneLength = 5, verbose = FALSE)

cm_gbm <- confusionMatrix(predict(gbm_model, valid), factor(valid$classe))
cm_gbm
```

## Model selection

```{r compare}
data.frame(
  model    = c("Decision tree", "Random forest", "Gradient boosting"),
  accuracy = c(cm_tree$overall["Accuracy"], cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"],
               cm_gbm$overall["Accuracy"]),
  oos_error = 1 - c(cm_tree$overall["Accuracy"], cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"],
                    cm_gbm$overall["Accuracy"])
)
```

The **random forest** performs best, with about 99.3% validation accuracy. That gives an expected out-of-sample error of about **0.7%**, so it is used for the final predictions.

## Predictor correlations

```{r corr, fig.width=9, fig.height=9}
correlation <- cor(train[, -ncol(train)])
corrplot(correlation, method = "color", tl.cex = 0.5, tl.col = "black")
```

## Predictions on the 20 test cases

```{r predict}
predicted <- predict(rf_model, test_set)
predicted
```

The random forest predicts: `r paste(predicted, collapse = " ")`.
